# Module 5 · Lesson 1 — Vector Databases

> **Time:** 3.5 h · **Prereq:** Module 3 (embeddings), Module 1 L3 (cosine similarity) · **Deliverable:** brute-force vs ANN benchmark

---

## 1. Detailed Description

### 1.1 What problem they solve

Module 1 Lesson 3 built a semantic search engine as a single matrix-vector product: stack `N` document embeddings into `D:(N, d)`, compute `D @ q`, take the top-k. That works perfectly — until `N` gets large.

```
N = 10,000      768-dim float32    →  30 MB,   ~5 ms per query.  Fine.
N = 10,000,000  768-dim float32    →  30 GB,   ~5 s per query.   Not fine.
```

A vector database solves three problems at once:
1. **Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search** — sublinear query time.
2. **Persistence and updates** — insert, delete, and update without rebuilding.
3. **Metadata filtering** — "find similar documents *written after 2025 by the legal team*."

### 1.2 Embeddings: the input

An embedding model maps text to `ℝ^d` such that semantically similar text lands nearby. The critical property is that this is **not** lexical matching — "car" and "automobile" are close, "bank" (finance) and "bank" (river) are far.

| Model | Dim | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 384 | tiny, fast, runs on CPU, surprisingly strong |
| `all-mpnet-base-v2` | 768 | better quality, still local |
| `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 768 | strong open model; needs a query prefix |
| `intfloat/e5-base-v2` | 768 | needs `"query: "` / `"passage: "` prefixes |
| `text-embedding-3-small` | 1536 | API, cheap, supports dimension truncation |
| `text-embedding-3-large` | 3072 | API, best-in-class general purpose |

**Two things that silently destroy retrieval quality:**

**Asymmetric prefixes.** Models like E5 and BGE were trained with instruction prefixes. If you embed passages with `"passage: "` and queries with no prefix — or vice versa — quality drops sharply with no error. Read the model card.

**Mixing models.** Embeddings from different models are in different spaces. Index with one model and query with another and you get noise. Store the model name in your index metadata and assert on it.

### 1.3 Distance metrics

```
cosine     = 1 − (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖)       # angle only, ignores magnitude
dot product= a·b                       # magnitude matters
L2         = ‖a − b‖₂                  # Euclidean
```

**On L2-normalised vectors these are monotonically equivalent** — `‖a−b‖² = 2 − 2(a·b)` when `‖a‖=‖b‖=1`. So the ranking is identical, which is why most vector DBs normalise on ingest and use dot product internally (it's the cheapest).

Use cosine unless you have a specific reason. Use dot product when magnitude encodes something meaningful (some models encode confidence in norm).

### 1.4 ANN indexes — how sublinear search works

**Flat (brute force).** Compare against everything. Exact, `O(N·d)`. Perfectly fine below ~100k vectors, and it is the baseline you must measure against.

**HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)** — the dominant algorithm.

Build a multi-layer graph. The top layer is sparse with long-range links; lower layers are dense with short-range links. Search starts at the top, greedily walks toward the query, then descends a layer and repeats. It is a skip-list for metric spaces.

| Parameter | Effect |
|---|---|
| `M` | links per node. Higher = better recall, more memory. 16–64 typical |
| `ef_construction` | search breadth during build. Higher = better index, slower build. 100–500 |
| `ef_search` | search breadth at query time. **Tunable per query** — the recall/latency dial |

`ef_search` is the knob you actually turn in production. Raise it until recall is acceptable, then stop.

**IVF (Inverted File)** — cluster vectors with k-means into `nlist` cells; at query time search only the `nprobe` nearest cells. Lower memory than HNSW, worse recall at the same speed. Often combined with PQ.

**PQ (Product Quantisation)** — split each vector into `m` sub-vectors, quantise each to one of 256 centroids. A 768-dim float32 vector (3,072 bytes) becomes ~96 bytes — a 32× compression. Lossy, so recall drops; used when memory is the binding constraint.

**ScaNN, DiskANN** — Google's anisotropic quantisation and Microsoft's SSD-resident index, respectively. Relevant at very large scale.

### 1.5 The recall/latency trade-off

ANN is *approximate*. Recall@k is the fraction of true top-k neighbours the index actually returns.

```
recall@10 = |returned_top10 ∩ true_top10| / 10
```

**Always measure recall against a brute-force baseline on a sample.** A team once spent weeks debugging "bad RAG" that turned out to be an index tuned to 60% recall. The retrieval was fine; the index was losing the right documents before the retriever saw them.

### 1.6 Metadata filtering, and why it's harder than it looks

"Find similar documents where `department = 'legal'` and `year >= 2024`."

Two naive approaches, both bad:
- **Pre-filter then search**: filter to the subset, then brute-force. Fine if the filter is very selective, catastrophic if it isn't.
- **Post-filter**: ANN search for top-100, then filter. If only 2 of the 100 match your filter, you get 2 results when you asked for 10.

Good vector DBs do **filtered ANN** — the graph traversal itself respects the filter, or they maintain per-filter indexes. When evaluating a vector DB, ask specifically how it handles filtering; it is where implementations differ most.

### 1.7 Choosing a vector database

| Database | Type | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Chroma** | embedded / server | prototyping, small-medium apps, this course |
| **FAISS** | library (no server) | research, custom pipelines, max control |
| **Qdrant** | server, Rust | strong filtering, good defaults, self-host |
| **Weaviate** | server | hybrid search, GraphQL, modules |
| **Milvus** | distributed | billion-scale |
| **pgvector** | Postgres extension | **you already have Postgres** |
| **Pinecone** | managed SaaS | no ops team |
| **Elasticsearch / OpenSearch** | search engine | you already run it; strong hybrid |

**The advice most likely to save you effort:** if you already run Postgres and have under ~5 million vectors, use **pgvector**. One less system to operate, transactional consistency with your relational data, and filtering is just SQL. The specialist databases earn their place at scale or when you need features they have and Postgres doesn't.

### 1.8 Hybrid search — the thing production systems actually do

Dense embeddings fail on exact terms: product codes, error numbers, names, rare jargon. BM25 fails on paraphrase. **Combine them.**

**Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** merges ranked lists without needing comparable scores:
```
RRF(d) = Σ_r  1 / (k + rank_r(d)),     k ≈ 60
```
Only ranks matter, so you never have to normalise a BM25 score against a cosine similarity — which is good, because there is no principled way to do that.

Module 4 Lesson 9 built the BM25 half. This module builds the dense half. Lesson 4 combines them.

---

## 2. Code Snippet

### 2.1 Embeddings, and the prefix trap

```python
# pip install sentence-transformers
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

docs = [
    "The transformer architecture uses self-attention.",
    "Python is a high-level programming language.",
    "Attention mechanisms let models focus on relevant tokens.",
    "Snakes are legless reptiles found on every continent except Antarctica.",
]
emb = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)
print(emb.shape, "norms:", np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1).round(4))

q = model.encode(["how do neural networks attend to input?"], normalize_embeddings=True)
scores = emb @ q.T                      # cosine, because everything is normalised
for s, d in sorted(zip(scores.ravel(), docs), reverse=True):
    print(f"{s:.4f}  {d}")
```

**Now the prefix trap, demonstrated:**

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

e5 = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/e5-base-v2")
passages = ["Deploys run every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.",
            "The cafeteria serves lunch from noon."]
query = "when do we deploy?"

# WRONG — no prefixes
p_wrong = e5.encode(passages, normalize_embeddings=True)
q_wrong = e5.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)

# RIGHT — the prefixes the model was trained with
p_right = e5.encode([f"passage: {p}" for p in passages], normalize_embeddings=True)
q_right = e5.encode([f"query: {query}"], normalize_embeddings=True)

print("without prefixes:", (p_wrong @ q_wrong.T).ravel().round(4))
print("with prefixes   :", (p_right @ q_right.T).ravel().round(4))
# The gap between the correct and incorrect document widens with prefixes.
```

### 2.2 Brute force — the baseline you must always have

```python
import numpy as np

class BruteForceIndex:
    """Exact search. Your ground truth for measuring ANN recall."""
    def __init__(self, dim):
        self.dim = dim
        self.vectors = np.zeros((0, dim), dtype=np.float32)
        self.ids = []

    def add(self, vectors, ids):
        v = np.asarray(vectors, dtype=np.float32)
        v /= np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12
        self.vectors = np.vstack([self.vectors, v])
        self.ids.extend(ids)

    def search(self, query, k=10):
        q = np.asarray(query, dtype=np.float32).ravel()
        q /= np.linalg.norm(q) + 1e-12
        scores = self.vectors @ q
        top = np.argpartition(-scores, min(k, len(scores) - 1))[:k]
        top = top[np.argsort(-scores[top])]
        return [(self.ids[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = BruteForceIndex(128)
idx.add(rng.standard_normal((5000, 128)), [f"doc{i}" for i in range(5000)])
print(idx.search(rng.standard_normal(128), k=5))
```

### 2.3 HNSW, and measuring what approximation costs you

```python
# pip install hnswlib
import hnswlib, numpy as np, time

DIM, N, K = 128, 100_000, 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = rng.standard_normal((N, DIM)).astype(np.float32)
data /= np.linalg.norm(data, axis=1, keepdims=True)
queries = rng.standard_normal((100, DIM)).astype(np.float32)
queries /= np.linalg.norm(queries, axis=1, keepdims=True)

# ---- ground truth (brute force)
t0 = time.time()
true_scores = queries @ data.T
true_top = np.argsort(-true_scores, axis=1)[:, :K]
brute_time = (time.time() - t0) / len(queries)

# ---- build HNSW
index = hnswlib.Index(space="cosine", dim=DIM)
t0 = time.time()
index.init_index(max_elements=N, ef_construction=200, M=16)
index.add_items(data, np.arange(N))
build_time = time.time() - t0
print(f"build: {build_time:.1f}s")

# ---- sweep ef_search: the recall/latency dial
print(f"\n{'ef':>6}{'recall@10':>12}{'ms/query':>12}{'speedup':>10}")
for ef in (10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400):
    index.set_ef(ef)
    t0 = time.time()
    labels, _ = index.knn_query(queries, k=K)
    ann_time = (time.time() - t0) / len(queries)
    recall = np.mean([len(set(labels[i]) & set(true_top[i])) / K
                      for i in range(len(queries))])
    print(f"{ef:>6}{recall:>12.4f}{ann_time*1000:>12.3f}{brute_time/ann_time:>9.0f}×")
print(f"\nbrute force: {brute_time*1000:.2f} ms/query")
```

**Expected output shape:**
```
    ef   recall@10    ms/query   speedup
    10      0.7850       0.045      310×
    20      0.9120       0.068      205×
    50      0.9760       0.130      107×
   100      0.9930       0.225       62×
   200      0.9985       0.410       34×
   400      0.9998       0.780       18×

brute force: 13.95 ms/query
```

Read this table carefully. At `ef=50` you get 97.6% recall at 107× the speed. At `ef=400` you get near-perfect recall and still 18× the speed. **Choose deliberately**; the default in most libraries is not tuned for your data.

### 2.4 Metadata filtering, three ways

```python
import numpy as np

class FilteredIndex:
    def __init__(self, dim):
        self.dim, self.vectors, self.meta, self.ids = dim, [], [], []

    def add(self, vec, id_, metadata):
        v = np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32)
        self.vectors.append(v / (np.linalg.norm(v) + 1e-12))
        self.ids.append(id_); self.meta.append(metadata)

    def _matches(self, m, flt):
        for key, cond in flt.items():
            val = m.get(key)
            if isinstance(cond, dict):
                for op, target in cond.items():
                    if op == "$gte" and not (val is not None and val >= target): return False
                    if op == "$lte" and not (val is not None and val <= target): return False
                    if op == "$in"  and val not in target: return False
                    if op == "$ne"  and val == target: return False
            elif val != cond:
                return False
        return True

    def search_prefilter(self, q, k=5, flt=None):
        """Filter first, then exact search. Good when the filter is selective."""
        keep = [i for i, m in enumerate(self.meta) if not flt or self._matches(m, flt)]
        if not keep: return []
        V = np.stack([self.vectors[i] for i in keep])
        q = np.asarray(q, np.float32); q /= np.linalg.norm(q) + 1e-12
        scores = V @ q
        order = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
        return [(self.ids[keep[i]], float(scores[i])) for i in order]

    def search_postfilter(self, q, k=5, flt=None, fetch=50):
        """Search first, then filter. FAILS when the filter is selective."""
        V = np.stack(self.vectors)
        q = np.asarray(q, np.float32); q /= np.linalg.norm(q) + 1e-12
        scores = V @ q
        cand = np.argsort(-scores)[:fetch]
        out = [(self.ids[i], float(scores[i])) for i in cand
               if not flt or self._matches(self.meta[i], flt)]
        return out[:k]

# demonstrate the post-filter failure mode
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = FilteredIndex(64)
for i in range(1000):
    idx.add(rng.standard_normal(64), f"doc{i}",
            {"dept": "legal" if i % 100 == 0 else "eng", "year": 2023 + i % 3})

q = rng.standard_normal(64)
flt = {"dept": "legal"}                 # only 1% of documents match
print("pre-filter  (correct):", len(idx.search_prefilter(q, k=5, flt=flt)))
print("post-filter (broken) :", len(idx.search_postfilter(q, k=5, flt=flt, fetch=50)))
# post-filter returns ~0-1 results instead of 5
```

### 2.5 Product quantisation — see the compression/recall trade

```python
# pip install faiss-cpu
import faiss, numpy as np, time

DIM, N = 128, 50_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = rng.standard_normal((N, DIM)).astype(np.float32)
faiss.normalize_L2(data)
queries = data[:100].copy()

configs = [
    ("Flat (exact)",  faiss.IndexFlatIP(DIM),                       DIM * 4),
    ("IVF256",        faiss.index_factory(DIM, "IVF256,Flat",
                                          faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT), DIM * 4),
    ("IVF256,PQ16",   faiss.index_factory(DIM, "IVF256,PQ16",
                                          faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT), 16),
    ("HNSW32",        faiss.index_factory(DIM, "HNSW32",
                                          faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT), DIM * 4 + 32 * 8),
]

truth = faiss.IndexFlatIP(DIM); truth.add(data)
_, true_ids = truth.search(queries, 10)

print(f"{'index':<16}{'bytes/vec':>11}{'recall@10':>12}{'ms/query':>11}")
for name, index, bytes_per in configs:
    if not index.is_trained:
        index.train(data)
    index.add(data)
    if hasattr(index, "nprobe"):
        index.nprobe = 16
    t0 = time.time(); _, ids = index.search(queries, 10)
    ms = (time.time() - t0) / len(queries) * 1000
    recall = np.mean([len(set(ids[i]) & set(true_ids[i])) / 10 for i in range(len(queries))])
    print(f"{name:<16}{bytes_per:>11}{recall:>12.4f}{ms:>11.3f}")
```

PQ16 stores 16 bytes per vector instead of 512 — a 32× reduction — and you pay in recall. That trade is the entire point of quantisation.

### 2.6 Cost and capacity planning

```python
def vector_db_cost(n_vectors, dim=768, dtype_bytes=4, index="hnsw", M=16,
                   replication=2, gb_month_usd=0.10):
    raw = n_vectors * dim * dtype_bytes
    if index == "hnsw":
        overhead = n_vectors * M * 2 * 8          # graph links
    elif index == "ivf_pq":
        raw = n_vectors * 16                       # PQ compressed
        overhead = raw * 0.1
    else:
        overhead = 0
    total_gb = (raw + overhead) * replication / 1e9
    print(f"{n_vectors:>12,} vectors, {dim}d, {index}")
    print(f"   raw vectors : {raw/1e9:8.2f} GB")
    print(f"   index over. : {overhead/1e9:8.2f} GB")
    print(f"   × {replication} replicas: {total_gb:8.2f} GB  ≈ ${total_gb*gb_month_usd:.2f}/month")
    return total_gb

for n in (100_000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000, 100_000_000):
    vector_db_cost(n)
    print()
```

Run this before choosing a database. A 100M-vector 768-dim HNSW index needs roughly 640 GB of RAM with replication — which immediately tells you whether you need quantisation or a disk-based index.

---

## 3. Use Case — an e-commerce search rebuild, and what actually moved the metric

A retailer replaced keyword search with vector search on 2 million products. Semantic search handled "comfortable shoes for standing all day" beautifully. Then support tickets spiked.

**What broke:**
- **Exact SKU lookups failed.** A customer searching `"WH-1000XM5"` got semantically similar headphones but not that one. Embeddings do not preserve alphanumeric identity.
- **Negation was ignored.** "Laptop without a touchscreen" returned touchscreen laptops. Embedding models are famously poor at negation.
- **Filters were post-applied**, so "red shoes under $50" returned three results instead of twenty.

**The fix — and the ordering matters:**
1. **Hybrid retrieval with RRF.** BM25 catches SKUs and exact model numbers; dense catches intent. This was the single biggest win.
2. **Filtered ANN**, not post-filtering. Moved to a database that supports it natively.
3. **Query classification.** A cheap classifier routes: looks like a SKU → lexical only; natural-language description → hybrid.
4. **A reranker** (Lesson 4) on the top 50 fused results.

**The measured outcome pattern:** hybrid alone recovered the exact-match regression and improved click-through over both pure-lexical and pure-dense. The reranker added a further gain at a latency cost they had to budget for.

**The generalisable lesson: dense retrieval is a *complement* to lexical search, not a replacement.** Anyone selling you pure vector search for a catalogue with identifiers has not run the exact-match tests.

---

## 4. Worked Example — build a semantic index and find where it fails

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

corpus = [
    "The deployment pipeline runs every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.",
    "Error code E4092 indicates a database connection timeout.",
    "To roll back a release, the on-call engineer runs make rollback.",
    "Our Python style guide requires type hints on all public functions.",
    "The staging environment mirrors production but uses synthetic data.",
    "Incident severity SEV-1 requires paging the on-call within 5 minutes.",
]
emb = model.encode(corpus, normalize_embeddings=True)

def search(query, k=3):
    q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)
    scores = (emb @ q.T).ravel()
    order = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [(round(float(scores[i]), 4), corpus[i]) for i in order]
```

**Query 1 — paraphrase. Dense search shines.**
```
"when are releases pushed out?"
  0.5821  The deployment pipeline runs every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.
  0.2914  To roll back a release, the on-call engineer runs make rollback.
  0.1102  The staging environment mirrors production...
```
No shared content words with the top result except "release" in a *different* document. Pure keyword search would have ranked the rollback document first. This is the win.

**Query 2 — exact identifier. Dense search fails.**
```
"E4092"
  0.2103  Error code E4092 indicates a database connection timeout.
  0.1854  Incident severity SEV-1 requires paging the on-call...
  0.1502  The deployment pipeline runs every Tuesday...
```
It got the right answer, but look at the **margin**: 0.21 vs 0.19. Nearly indistinguishable. Add 10,000 more documents and this ranking becomes a coin flip. BM25 would score this 8.4 vs 0.0 — an unambiguous match.

**Query 3 — negation. Dense search fails badly.**
```
"deployments that do NOT happen on Tuesday"
  0.5403  The deployment pipeline runs every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.
```
The single most wrong document is ranked first. The embedding encodes the *topic*, not the logical operator. **No amount of index tuning fixes this** — it is a property of the embedding model.

### What this tells you to build

| Query type | Dense | BM25 | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paraphrase | ✓✓ | ✗ | dense |
| Exact ID / code | weak margin | ✓✓ | lexical |
| Negation | ✗ | ✗ | neither — needs an LLM or structured filter |
| Multi-concept | ✓ | partial | hybrid |

**Hybrid retrieval is not an optimisation, it is a correctness requirement** for any corpus containing identifiers. And negation needs a different mechanism entirely — usually query rewriting by an LLM into a filter, which Lesson 4 covers.

**Measure the margin, not just the rank.** A correct top-1 with a 0.02 score gap is a result that will break as your corpus grows. Log score distributions in production.

---

## 5. Practice

1. Run §2.1 and confirm you can reproduce the E5 prefix gap. Then do the same for a BGE model — read its model card to find the required prefix.
2. **Recall sweep.** Run §2.3 at `N ∈ {10k, 100k, 1M}`. Plot recall@10 vs ms/query for each. At what N does brute force stop being viable for a 50 ms latency budget?
3. Tune HNSW's build parameters: `M ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64}` × `ef_construction ∈ {100, 200, 400}`. Report build time, memory and recall at fixed `ef_search=50`. Which parameter matters most?
4. **Reproduce the post-filter failure** (§2.4) and plot the number of results returned vs filter selectivity from 50% down to 0.1%. This is the graph that justifies filtered ANN.
5. Run the FAISS comparison (§2.5). Add `IVF256,PQ32` and `IVF256,PQ64`. Plot recall vs bytes-per-vector. Where's the knee?
6. **Model comparison.** Index the same 1,000 documents with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `all-mpnet-base-v2` and `bge-base-en-v1.5`. Build 30 query/relevant-doc pairs and report recall@5 for each. Include embedding time and index size.
7. Reproduce the §4 failure cases on your own corpus. Find one paraphrase query where dense wins decisively and one exact-match query where it nearly fails. Report the score margins.
8. **Capacity planning.** Using §2.6, work out the infrastructure for 50M documents at 1536 dimensions. Then recompute with `text-embedding-3-small` truncated to 512 dimensions. How much does dimension truncation save, and what does it cost in recall? (Test it.)
9. Implement RRF fusion of a dense and a BM25 ranking. Verify on the §4 corpus that it gets both the paraphrase query and the `E4092` query right.

---

## 6. Resources

**Papers**
- Malkov & Yashunin, *HNSW* — https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320
- Jégou et al., *Product Quantization for NN Search* — https://inria.hal.science/inria-00514462
- Johnson et al., *Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (FAISS)* — https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734
- Karpukhin et al., *Dense Passage Retrieval* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906
- Cormack et al., *Reciprocal Rank Fusion* — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1571941.1572114
- Wang et al., *Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (E5)* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03533
- Muennighoff et al., *MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316

**Tools**
- MTEB leaderboard — https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard
- sentence-transformers — https://sbert.net/
- FAISS — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss
- hnswlib — https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib
- ANN-Benchmarks — https://ann-benchmarks.com/
- pgvector — https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector

**Reading**
- Pinecone learning centre — https://www.pinecone.io/learn/
- Chroma cookbook — https://cookbook.chromadb.dev/

lessons.md:
# Module 5 · Lesson 2 — ChromaDB

> **Time:** 3 h · **Prereq:** Lesson 1 · **Deliverable:** a persistent, filtered, versioned collection

---

## 1. Detailed Description

### 1.1 Why Chroma

Chroma is an embedded-first vector database: `pip install chromadb` and you have a working store with no server, no Docker, no config. It uses SQLite for persistence and HNSW for search. Apache 2.0 licensed.

It is the right choice for learning and for small-to-medium production. Below a few million vectors on a single node it is entirely adequate. Above that, or when you need horizontal scaling and heavy concurrent writes, look at Qdrant, Milvus or pgvector.

### 1.2 Client modes

```python
import chromadb

chromadb.Client()                                    # in-memory, lost on exit
chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")        # local disk — the usual choice
chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost", port=8000)     # connect to `chroma run`
chromadb.CloudClient(...)                            # hosted
```

**Important change from older tutorials:** there is no `.persist()` call any more. `PersistentClient` writes as you go. If you find `client.persist()` or `vectordb.persist()` in a tutorial, it is pre-0.4 and out of date.

### 1.3 Collections

A collection is a named set of documents with embeddings, metadata and IDs. Four things you set at creation and cannot change later without recreating:

- **`name`** — 3–63 chars, alphanumeric plus `_` and `-`, must start and end alphanumeric (it appears in REST URLs).
- **`embedding_function`** — how text becomes vectors. **This is sticky.** Create with one model and query with another and you get silent nonsense.
- **`metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}`** — the distance metric. Default is `l2`; you almost always want `cosine`.
- **HNSW parameters** — `hnsw:construction_ef`, `hnsw:M`, `hnsw:search_ef`.

```python
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="docs",
    embedding_function=ef,
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine", "hnsw:construction_ef": 200, "hnsw:M": 16},
)
```

### 1.4 The four core operations

```python
collection.add(ids=[...], documents=[...], metadatas=[...], embeddings=[...])
collection.query(query_texts=[...], n_results=5, where={...}, where_document={...})
collection.get(ids=[...], where={...}, limit=100)
collection.update(ids=[...], documents=[...])   # or .upsert(), or .delete()
```

**IDs are your idempotency mechanism.** `add` with an existing ID raises; `upsert` replaces. Deterministic IDs — a hash of `(source_file, chunk_index)` — mean you can re-run ingestion safely. Random UUIDs mean every re-run duplicates your corpus. This is the single most common Chroma mistake.

### 1.5 Distances, not similarities

`query` returns **distances**, where lower is better. With `hnsw:space = "cosine"`:
```
distance = 1 − cosine_similarity        → range [0, 2]
similarity = 1 − distance
```
People routinely mistake distance for similarity and build thresholds backwards. Convert explicitly and name your variables accordingly.

### 1.6 Metadata filtering

Chroma supports MongoDB-style operators:

```python
where={"year": {"$gte": 2024}}
where={"$and": [{"dept": "legal"}, {"year": {"$gte": 2024}}]}
where={"$or": [{"type": "policy"}, {"type": "runbook"}]}
where={"status": {"$in": ["published", "reviewed"]}}
```
Operators: `$eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin $and $or`.

Metadata values must be **scalars** — `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`. No lists, no nested dicts. To filter on a list, either flatten to booleans (`{"tag_legal": True}`) or join to a string and use `where_document` substring matching.

`where_document={"$contains": "rollback"}` filters on the document text itself — a crude but useful lexical filter.

### 1.7 Embedding functions

```python
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

# default: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, downloaded and run locally
default_ef = embedding_functions.DefaultEmbeddingFunction()

st_ef = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-mpnet-base-v2")

openai_ef = embedding_functions.OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"], model_name="text-embedding-3-small")
```

Or bypass entirely and pass `embeddings=` directly to `add()` — necessary when you need prefix handling (Lesson 1 §1.2) or a custom pipeline.

### 1.8 Operational notes

- **Batch your adds.** 100–500 documents per call. One-at-a-time is dramatically slower.
- **`collection.count()`** after ingest, always. It catches silent failures.
- **Back up** by copying the persist directory while nothing is writing.
- **Concurrency:** `PersistentClient` uses SQLite; multiple processes writing to the same path will fight. Use `chroma run` and `HttpClient` for multi-process access.
- **Versioning:** put the embedding model name in the collection name or metadata. When you upgrade models you must reindex, and you want that to be obvious rather than a mystery quality regression.

---

## 2. Code Snippet

### 2.1 The essentials, end to end

```python
import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")

ef = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="engineering_docs",
    embedding_function=ef,
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"},        # NOT the default — set it explicitly
)

collection.add(
    ids=["runbook-0", "runbook-1", "style-0", "incident-0"],
    documents=[
        "Production deployments run every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.",
        "To roll back, the on-call engineer runs `make rollback` from the release branch.",
        "All public functions require type hints. Line length is 100 characters.",
        "SEV-1 incidents require paging the on-call within 5 minutes.",
    ],
    metadatas=[
        {"doc": "runbook.md", "team": "platform", "year": 2026, "reviewed": True},
        {"doc": "runbook.md", "team": "platform", "year": 2026, "reviewed": True},
        {"doc": "style.md",   "team": "platform", "year": 2025, "reviewed": True},
        {"doc": "incident.md","team": "sre",      "year": 2026, "reviewed": False},
    ],
)
print("count:", collection.count())

res = collection.query(query_texts=["when do we ship releases?"], n_results=3)

for doc, meta, dist in zip(res["documents"][0], res["metadatas"][0], res["distances"][0]):
    print(f"sim={1-dist:.4f}  [{meta['doc']}]  {doc[:70]}")
```

### 2.2 Deterministic IDs — make ingestion idempotent

```python
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

def chunk_id(source: str, index: int, text: str) -> str:
    """Stable across runs. Changes only if the content changes."""
    h = hashlib.sha256(f"{source}|{index}|{text}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
    return f"{Path(source).stem}-{index:04d}-{h}"

# Re-running ingestion with upsert is now safe and idempotent
collection.upsert(
    ids=[chunk_id("runbook.md", 0, text)],
    documents=[text],
    metadatas=[{"doc": "runbook.md", "chunk": 0}],
)
```

Compare with the anti-pattern:
```python
import uuid
collection.add(ids=[str(uuid.uuid4())], documents=[text])   # ← every re-run duplicates
```

### 2.3 Filtering

```python
# metadata filter
res = collection.query(
    query_texts=["deployment process"],
    n_results=5,
    where={"$and": [{"team": "platform"}, {"year": {"$gte": 2026}}]},
)

# document-text filter (substring)
res = collection.query(
    query_texts=["how to undo a release"],
    n_results=5,
    where_document={"$contains": "rollback"},
)

# combined
res = collection.query(
    query_texts=["incident response"],
    n_results=5,
    where={"reviewed": True},
    where_document={"$contains": "SEV"},
)

# fetch without searching
everything = collection.get(where={"team": "sre"}, limit=100,
                            include=["documents", "metadatas"])
print(f"{len(everything['ids'])} SRE documents")
```

### 2.4 A production-shaped ingestion pipeline

```python
"""Chunk, embed, upsert — with batching, idempotency and verification."""
import hashlib, re
from pathlib import Path
import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

EMBED_MODEL = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_OVERLAP, BATCH = 800, 120, 200


def split_markdown(text: str, size: int, overlap: int) -> list[str]:
    """Split on paragraph boundaries, falling back to hard cuts."""
    paras = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r"\n\s*\n", text) if p.strip()]
    chunks, buf = [], ""
    for p in paras:
        if len(buf) + len(p) + 2 <= size:
            buf = f"{buf}\n\n{p}" if buf else p
        else:
            if buf:
                chunks.append(buf)
                buf = (buf[-overlap:] + "\n\n" + p) if overlap else p
            else:
                buf = p
            while len(buf) > size:
                chunks.append(buf[:size])
                buf = buf[size - overlap:]
    if buf:
        chunks.append(buf)
    return chunks


def ingest(data_dir: str, persist_dir: str = "./chroma_db",
           collection_name: str | None = None):
    # encode the model in the collection name so a model change is visible
    collection_name = collection_name or f"docs__{EMBED_MODEL.replace('/', '_')}"

    client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=persist_dir)
    ef = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name=EMBED_MODEL)
    col = client.get_or_create_collection(
        name=collection_name, embedding_function=ef,
        metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine", "hnsw:construction_ef": 200, "hnsw:M": 16},
    )

    ids, docs, metas = [], [], []
    n_files = 0
    for path in sorted(Path(data_dir).rglob("*")):
        if path.suffix.lower() not in {".md", ".txt"}:
            continue
        n_files += 1
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")
        for i, chunk in enumerate(split_markdown(text, CHUNK_SIZE, CHUNK_OVERLAP)):
            h = hashlib.sha256(f"{path.name}|{i}|{chunk}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
            ids.append(f"{path.stem}-{i:04d}-{h}")
            docs.append(chunk)
            metas.append({
                "source": path.name,
                "path": str(path),
                "chunk_index": i,
                "chars": len(chunk),
                "embed_model": EMBED_MODEL,          # ← provenance
            })

    before = col.count()
    for s in range(0, len(ids), BATCH):
        col.upsert(ids=ids[s:s+BATCH], documents=docs[s:s+BATCH],
                   metadatas=metas[s:s+BATCH])
        print(f"  upserted {min(s+BATCH, len(ids))}/{len(ids)}", end="\r")

    after = col.count()
    print(f"\n{n_files} files → {len(ids)} chunks. collection: {before} → {after}")

    # verification: re-running must NOT change the count
    assert after >= before
    return col


if __name__ == "__main__":
    col = ingest("./data")
    print(col.query(query_texts=["test query"], n_results=2)["ids"])
```

### 2.5 Distance → similarity, and thresholding

```python
def search(collection, query: str, k: int = 5, min_similarity: float = 0.25,
           where: dict | None = None):
    """Returns (similarity, document, metadata), filtered by a similarity FLOOR.

    The floor is what lets your app say "I don't know" instead of answering
    from irrelevant context. See Module 4 Lesson 9 §3.3.
    """
    res = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=k, where=where,
                           include=["documents", "metadatas", "distances"])
    out = []
    for doc, meta, dist in zip(res["documents"][0], res["metadatas"][0],
                               res["distances"][0]):
        sim = 1.0 - dist                    # cosine space only
        if sim >= min_similarity:
            out.append((sim, doc, meta))
    return out


hits = search(collection, "how do I undo a bad deploy?", k=5)
if not hits:
    print("No relevant documents found.")
for sim, doc, meta in hits:
    print(f"{sim:.4f}  [{meta['source']}]  {doc[:80]}")
```

**Calibrate `min_similarity` on your own data.** Run 20 queries you know are answerable and 20 you know are not, plot the two score distributions, and pick the threshold that separates them. A value copied from a tutorial is meaningless for your corpus and embedding model.

### 2.6 LangChain integration

```python
# pip install langchain-chroma
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_core.documents import Document

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

vectorstore = Chroma(
    collection_name="langchain_docs",
    embedding_function=embeddings,
    persist_directory="./chroma_langchain",
    collection_metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"},
)

docs = [
    Document(page_content="Deploys run Tuesdays at 14:00 UTC.",
             metadata={"source": "runbook.md", "team": "platform"}),
    Document(page_content="SEV-1 pages the on-call within 5 minutes.",
             metadata={"source": "incident.md", "team": "sre"}),
]
vectorstore.add_documents(docs, ids=["runbook-0", "incident-0"])   # explicit IDs

# with scores — note these are DISTANCES
for doc, score in vectorstore.similarity_search_with_score("when do we deploy?", k=2):
    print(f"distance={score:.4f}  {doc.page_content[:60]}")

# as a retriever, for use in chains (Lesson 4)
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(
    search_type="similarity_score_threshold",
    search_kwargs={"k": 4, "score_threshold": 0.3, "filter": {"team": "platform"}},
)
```

**Attaching to an existing Chroma collection created outside LangChain:**
```python
import chromadb
from langchain_chroma import Chroma

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")
vs = Chroma(client=client, collection_name="engineering_docs",
            embedding_function=embeddings)
```

### 2.7 Client-server mode

```bash
chroma run --path ./chroma_db --port 8000
```
```python
import chromadb
client = chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost", port=8000)
print(client.heartbeat())
col = client.get_or_create_collection("docs")
```

Use this whenever more than one process touches the database — a Streamlit app that reloads, a worker plus an API, or anything containerised.

### 2.8 Maintenance

```python
# inspect
print([c.name for c in client.list_collections()])
print(collection.count())
print(collection.peek(3))

# delete specific documents
collection.delete(ids=["runbook-0"])
collection.delete(where={"source": "outdated.md"})     # by metadata

# reindex under a new embedding model — build the new one, then swap
new_col = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="docs__bge-base-en-v1.5", embedding_function=new_ef,
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"})
old = collection.get(include=["documents", "metadatas"])
for s in range(0, len(old["ids"]), 200):
    new_col.upsert(ids=old["ids"][s:s+200],
                   documents=old["documents"][s:s+200],
                   metadatas=old["metadatas"][s:s+200])

# destructive
client.delete_collection("old_collection")
```

---

## 3. Use Case — the reindex that broke search silently

A team upgraded their embedding model from MiniLM to a larger BGE model to improve quality. They changed the `embedding_function` and redeployed.

Search quality collapsed, and nothing errored.

**What happened:** the existing collection contained 384-dimensional MiniLM vectors. New documents were added with 768-dimensional BGE vectors. Chroma raised a dimension error for new adds — but queries against the *old* vectors used the *new* model's query embedding, producing meaningless similarities on the subset that still worked. Partial breakage is much harder to diagnose than total breakage.

**The fixes, which are cheap to adopt before you need them:**
1. **Encode the model in the collection name** — `docs__all-MiniLM-L6-v2`. A model change is now a visibly different collection, not a silent mutation.
2. **Store `embed_model` in every chunk's metadata.** Assert on it at query time.
3. **Blue/green reindexing.** Build the new collection alongside the old, run your eval set against both, then switch a config pointer. Never mutate in place.
4. **A canary eval** — 20 queries with known-correct answers, run on every deploy. This would have caught it in seconds.

**The general principle:** an embedding model is part of your schema. Treat a model upgrade like a database migration, with a version, a backfill and a rollback plan.

---

## 4. Worked Example — chunk size, measured

Chunking is the highest-leverage decision in the whole RAG pipeline, and almost everyone picks a number from a tutorial without testing it.

```python
"""Measure retrieval quality across chunk sizes."""
import chromadb, hashlib
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

DOCUMENT = open("data/runbook.md").read()

# 12 questions with the answer text that must appear in a retrieved chunk
EVAL = [
    ("When do production deploys run?",          "Tuesday at 14:00 UTC"),
    ("Who approves a rollback?",                 "on-call engineer"),
    ("What does error E4092 mean?",              "database connection timeout"),
    ("How fast must SEV-1 be acknowledged?",     "5 minutes"),
    # ... 8 more
]

def build(chunk_size, overlap, name):
    client = chromadb.Client()                       # in-memory for the experiment
    ef = embedding_functions.DefaultEmbeddingFunction()
    col = client.get_or_create_collection(name=name, embedding_function=ef,
                                          metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"})
    chunks = [DOCUMENT[i:i+chunk_size]
              for i in range(0, len(DOCUMENT), chunk_size - overlap)]
    col.add(ids=[f"c{i}" for i in range(len(chunks))], documents=chunks)
    return col, chunks

print(f"{'size':>6}{'overlap':>9}{'chunks':>8}{'hit@1':>8}{'hit@3':>8}{'tok@3':>8}")
for size in (200, 400, 800, 1500, 3000):
    overlap = size // 8
    col, chunks = build(size, overlap, f"c{size}")
    hit1 = hit3 = 0
    tokens = 0
    for question, answer in EVAL:
        res = col.query(query_texts=[question], n_results=3)
        docs = res["documents"][0]
        if answer.lower() in docs[0].lower():
            hit1 += 1
        if any(answer.lower() in d.lower() for d in docs):
            hit3 += 1
        tokens += sum(len(d) for d in docs) // 4
    n = len(EVAL)
    print(f"{size:>6}{overlap:>9}{len(chunks):>8}{hit1/n:>8.2f}{hit3/n:>8.2f}{tokens//n:>8}")
```

**Typical output:**
```
  size  overlap  chunks   hit@1   hit@3   tok@3
   200       25      89    0.42    0.67     150
   400       50      45    0.58    0.83     300
   800      100      23    0.75    1.00     600
  1500      187      12    0.83    1.00    1125
  3000      375       6    0.75    0.92    2250
```

### Reading this table

**Small chunks (200) lose context.** The answer "Tuesday at 14:00 UTC" may be split from the question it answers, or the chunk lacks the surrounding sentence that makes it retrievable. Hit@1 is poor.

**Large chunks (3000) dilute the embedding.** A single vector must represent 3,000 characters covering several topics. The embedding becomes an average of unrelated things and matches nothing precisely. Hit@1 *falls* from 1500 to 3000 — this non-monotonicity is the key finding and it surprises people.

**The sweet spot is task-dependent** but lands around 500–1500 characters for prose. Note the cost column: 1500-char chunks put 1,125 tokens into your prompt per query versus 600 at 800 chars. **1500 buys +0.08 hit@1 for ~2× the context cost.** Whether that's worth it depends on your token budget.

### What to take from this

1. **Run this experiment on your own corpus.** The optimum depends on your document structure — dense reference docs want smaller chunks, narrative prose wants larger.
2. **hit@3 saturating at 1.0 while hit@1 keeps improving** means your reranker (Lesson 4) has room to work. If hit@3 is 1.0, a reranker can get you to hit@1 = 1.0 without changing retrieval at all.
3. **Overlap matters most at small sizes.** At 200 chars with no overlap, answers spanning a boundary are unretrievable. At 1500, overlap is mostly wasted storage.
4. **Structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size.** Splitting on markdown headers keeps semantic units together. Lesson 4 covers this.

---

## 5. Practice

1. Build a persistent collection from your own documents using §2.4. Run the ingestion **twice** and verify `count()` is unchanged — proving idempotency.
2. Now break it: replace the deterministic ID with `uuid.uuid4()`, re-run, and watch the count double. Then fix it.
3. **Calibrate your threshold.** Run 20 answerable and 20 unanswerable queries. Plot both similarity distributions on one histogram. Pick `min_similarity`. Report the false-accept and false-reject rates at your chosen value.
4. Run the chunk-size experiment (§4) on your corpus with at least 12 eval questions. Produce the table and pick a size with a stated justification including token cost.
5. Add `chunk_overlap ∈ {0, 10%, 25%, 50%}` as a second dimension at your chosen chunk size. Does overlap help enough to justify the storage?
6. **Filtering.** Build a collection with `team`, `year` and `reviewed` metadata. Write five queries combining `$and`, `$or`, `$gte` and `$in`. Verify each returns only matching documents.
7. Compare `hnsw:space` of `cosine` vs `l2` vs `ip` on the same normalised embeddings. Confirm the rankings are identical (Lesson 1 §1.3) and explain why the distance *values* differ.
8. **Reindex safely.** Build collection A with MiniLM, then collection B with mpnet from the same source. Run your eval set against both. Report which wins and by how much — then decide whether the quality gain justifies the larger model's latency.
9. Start `chroma run` and connect with `HttpClient` from two separate Python processes simultaneously. Then try the same with two `PersistentClient`s on one path and observe the difference.
10. Measure ingestion throughput at batch sizes 1, 10, 100, 500. Plot documents-per-second.

---

**Docs**
- Chroma docs — https://docs.trychroma.com/
- Chroma cookbook (deeper, community) — https://cookbook.chromadb.dev/
- `langchain-chroma` — https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/vectorstores/chroma/
- Chroma GitHub — https://github.com/chroma-core/chroma

**Related**

**On chunking**
- Pinecone, *Chunking Strategies* — https://www.pinecone.io/learn/chunking-strategies/
- LangChain text splitters — https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/text_splitters/

# Module 5 · Lesson 3 — Applications of RAG

> **Time:** 3 h · **Prereq:** Lessons 1–2 · **Deliverable:** a RAG evaluation harness + architecture decision doc

---

## 1. Detailed Description

### 1.1 What RAG is and why it exists

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant documents, put them in the prompt, generate an answer grounded in them.

```
question → [retrieve] → context → [generate with context] → answer + citations
```

Lewis et al. (2020) introduced the term. The motivation is everything a parametric model is bad at:

| Problem | How RAG addresses it |
|---|---|
| Knowledge cutoff | retrieve current documents |
| Private data | retrieve from your corpus |
| Hallucination | ground answers in retrieved text |
| No citations | return sources with the answer |
| Expensive updates | re-index, don't retrain |
| No access control | filter retrieval by permission |

That last one is underrated. **You cannot give a fine-tuned model per-user permissions** — the knowledge is baked into the weights. With RAG, you filter the retrieval by the user's access rights and the model simply never sees documents they shouldn't. This alone disqualifies fine-tuning for most enterprise knowledge applications.

### 1.2 RAG vs fine-tuning — the decision, restated

Module 4 Lesson 1 framed this as **knowledge vs behaviour**. Restating with the retrieval lens:

| Signal | Answer |
|---|---|
| The facts change weekly | RAG |
| You need citations | RAG |
| Per-user access control | RAG |
| The corpus is larger than any context window | RAG |
| The model won't follow your format | fine-tune |
| The model won't adopt your tone | fine-tune |
| The model lacks domain *vocabulary* | fine-tune (or continued pretraining) |
| You need low latency and small models | fine-tune |

**They compose.** The strongest systems do both: RAG for facts, a light fine-tune for format and refusal behaviour.

### 1.3 The RAG failure taxonomy

Barnett et al. (2024) catalogued seven failure points. Knowing which one you have is most of the work:

| # | Failure | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Missing content** | corpus doesn't contain the answer | must refuse — test this |
| 2 | **Missed top-k** | answer exists but ranked below k | better retrieval, hybrid, higher k + rerank |
| 3 | **Not in consolidated context** | retrieved but dropped during reranking/truncation | check your context assembly |
| 4 | **Not extracted** | in context but model missed it | better prompt, "lost in the middle", smaller context |
| 5 | **Wrong format** | ignored output instructions | structured output, few-shot |
| 6 | **Incorrect specificity** | too vague or too detailed | prompt tuning, query classification |
| 7 | **Incomplete** | partial answer from partial retrieval | multi-query, higher k |

**Diagnose before you fix.** The single most common mistake is tuning the generation prompt when the problem is at failure point 2 — the right document never made it into the context. Always inspect what was retrieved before blaming the model.

### 1.4 Advanced patterns

**Query transformation**
- **Rewriting** — turn a conversational follow-up into a standalone query. Essential for multi-turn.
- **Multi-query** — generate 3–5 paraphrases, retrieve for each, union the results. Cheap and effective.
- **HyDE** — have the LLM write a *hypothetical answer*, embed that, and retrieve with it. Answers look like documents; questions don't. Often a large win on hard queries.
- **Decomposition** — split a multi-part question into sub-questions, retrieve for each.

**Retrieval improvements**
- **Hybrid (dense + BM25 with RRF)** — Lesson 1 §1.8. Do this by default.
- **Reranking** — retrieve 50 with a cheap bi-encoder, rerank with a cross-encoder, keep 5. Usually the highest-ROI single addition.
- **Parent-document retrieval** — index small chunks for precision, return their larger parent for context.
- **Contextual retrieval** — prepend an LLM-generated summary of the document to each chunk before embedding. Anthropic reported substantial retrieval-failure reductions from this plus hybrid plus reranking.

**Architecture patterns**
- **Self-RAG** — the model decides whether to retrieve at all and critiques what it gets.
- **Corrective RAG (CRAG)** — grade retrieved documents; if they're poor, fall back to web search.
- **Agentic RAG** — retrieval as a tool the agent can call repeatedly with refined queries.
- **GraphRAG** — build a knowledge graph over the corpus; good for "what connects X and Y" questions that no single chunk answers.

### 1.5 Evaluating RAG — separate the two halves

You must measure retrieval and generation **independently**, or you cannot tell which is broken.

**Retrieval metrics** (need labelled query → relevant-doc pairs):
```
recall@k     — fraction of relevant docs in the top k        ← the critical one
precision@k  — fraction of top k that are relevant
MRR          — mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant doc
nDCG@k       — rank-weighted, handles graded relevance
```
**Recall@k is the ceiling on your whole system.** If the answer isn't retrieved, no prompt engineering recovers it.

**Generation metrics** (the RAGAS framing):
```
faithfulness       — is every claim supported by the retrieved context?
answer relevance   — does it address the question?
context precision  — are the retrieved chunks actually useful?
context recall     — did retrieval get everything needed?
```

**And the metric most teams forget: refusal accuracy.** Include unanswerable questions in every eval set. A system that answers everything confidently is worse than one that admits gaps.

### 1.6 Real application patterns

| Application | Corpus | Retrieval notes |
|---|---|---|
| Internal knowledge assistant | wiki, docs, tickets | permission filtering is mandatory |
| Customer support | help centre, past tickets | hybrid — product names need lexical |
| Legal / contract Q&A | contracts, case law | citations are the product; use extractive where possible |
| Code assistant | repo, docs | AST-aware chunking beats text chunking |
| Research assistant | papers | section-aware chunking; metadata filtering by year/venue |
| Medical | literature, guidelines | faithfulness gate required (Module 4 L4 §3) |

### 1.7 Production concerns

- **Freshness** — incremental indexing, not nightly rebuilds. Deterministic IDs make this trivial (Lesson 2 §2.2).
- **Permissions** — filter at retrieval. Never rely on the prompt to withhold information the model can see.
- **Cost** — retrieval adds 1,000–4,000 tokens per query. Measure it.
- **Latency** — embed (~20 ms) + search (~10 ms) + rerank (~100 ms) + generate (~1–3 s).
- **PII** — scrub on ingest, not in the prompt.
- **Prompt injection via documents** — a malicious document in your corpus can instruct the model. Module 4 Lesson 6 §3 applies directly here.

---

## 2. Code Snippet

### 2.1 Retrieval evaluation — build this first

```python
"""Retrieval metrics. Run this BEFORE touching your generation prompt."""
import numpy as np
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class EvalQuery:
    question: str
    relevant_ids: set[str]              # ground-truth relevant chunk IDs
    answerable: bool = True

def recall_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, k):
    if not relevant_ids:
        return 1.0
    return len(set(retrieved_ids[:k]) & relevant_ids) / len(relevant_ids)

def precision_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, k):
    if k == 0:
        return 0.0
    return len(set(retrieved_ids[:k]) & relevant_ids) / k

def mrr(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids):
    for i, rid in enumerate(retrieved_ids, start=1):
        if rid in relevant_ids:
            return 1.0 / i
    return 0.0

def ndcg_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, k):
    dcg = sum(1.0 / np.log2(i + 1)
              for i, rid in enumerate(retrieved_ids[:k], start=1) if rid in relevant_ids)
    ideal = sum(1.0 / np.log2(i + 1)
                for i in range(1, min(len(relevant_ids), k) + 1))
    return dcg / ideal if ideal else 0.0


def evaluate_retrieval(retrieve_fn, queries: list[EvalQuery], ks=(1, 3, 5, 10)):
    """retrieve_fn(question, k) -> list of chunk IDs, ranked."""
    rows = []
    for q in queries:
        ids = retrieve_fn(q.question, max(ks))
        row = {"q": q.question, "mrr": mrr(ids, q.relevant_ids),
               "returned": len(ids), "answerable": q.answerable}
        for k in ks:
            row[f"r@{k}"] = recall_at_k(ids, q.relevant_ids, k)
            row[f"p@{k}"] = precision_at_k(ids, q.relevant_ids, k)
            row[f"ndcg@{k}"] = ndcg_at_k(ids, q.relevant_ids, k)
        rows.append(row)

    answerable = [r for r in rows if r["answerable"]]
    print(f"{'metric':<12}" + "".join(f"{f'k={k}':>9}" for k in ks))
    for name in ("r", "p", "ndcg"):
        vals = "".join(f"{np.mean([r[f'{name}@{k}'] for r in answerable]):>9.3f}" for k in ks)
        print(f"{name+'@k':<12}{vals}")
    print(f"\nMRR: {np.mean([r['mrr'] for r in answerable]):.4f}")

    # the refusal check
    unanswerable = [r for r in rows if not r["answerable"]]
    if unanswerable:
        empty = sum(1 for r in unanswerable if r["returned"] == 0)
        print(f"unanswerable queries returning nothing: {empty}/{len(unanswerable)}")
    return rows
```

### 2.2 Query transformation

```python
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)

# ---------- 1. query rewriting for multi-turn
rewrite_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "Rewrite the user's latest message as a standalone search query "
               "that makes sense without the conversation history. "
               "Output ONLY the query, nothing else. If it is already standalone, "
               "return it unchanged."),
    ("human", "Conversation:\n{history}\n\nLatest message: {question}"),
])
rewriter = rewrite_prompt | model | StrOutputParser()

print(rewriter.invoke({
    "history": "User: What's our deploy schedule?\nAssistant: Tuesdays at 14:00 UTC.",
    "question": "and who approves it?",
}))
# → "who approves the deployment schedule"   ← now retrievable on its own


# ---------- 2. multi-query expansion
class Queries(BaseModel):
    queries: list[str] = Field(description="3 diverse paraphrases of the question")

multiquery = (ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Generate 3 different phrasings of this question to maximise retrieval coverage. "
    "Vary the vocabulary.\n\nQuestion: {question}")
    | model.with_structured_output(Queries))

print(multiquery.invoke({"question": "how do I undo a bad release?"}).queries)


# ---------- 3. HyDE — embed a hypothetical ANSWER, not the question
hyde = (ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Write a short passage that would answer this question, as it might appear "
    "in internal documentation. Invent plausible specifics; accuracy doesn't matter, "
    "only that it looks like a real document.\n\nQuestion: {question}")
    | model | StrOutputParser())

hypothetical = hyde.invoke({"question": "what is our incident escalation policy?"})
print(hypothetical)
# Embed THIS, not the question. Documents look like documents.


# ---------- 4. decomposition
class SubQuestions(BaseModel):
    sub_questions: list[str]

decompose = (ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Break this into independent sub-questions that can each be answered by "
    "a single document. If it's already atomic, return it unchanged.\n\n{question}")
    | model.with_structured_output(SubQuestions))

print(decompose.invoke({
    "question": "How do our deploy schedule and rollback process compare to our SLA?"
}).sub_questions)
```

### 2.3 Hybrid retrieval with RRF

```python
"""Dense + BM25 fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion."""
import re
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

def tokenize(t): return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", t.lower())

class HybridRetriever:
    def __init__(self, collection, chunk_texts: dict[str, str]):
        self.collection = collection                 # Chroma collection (dense)
        self.ids = list(chunk_texts.keys())
        self.texts = [chunk_texts[i] for i in self.ids]
        self.bm25 = BM25Okapi([tokenize(t) for t in self.texts])

    def dense(self, query, k):
        res = self.collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=k)
        return res["ids"][0]

    def lexical(self, query, k):
        scores = self.bm25.get_scores(tokenize(query))
        order = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: -scores[i])[:k]
        return [self.ids[i] for i in order]

    def search(self, query, k=5, fetch=30, rrf_k=60, weights=(1.0, 1.0)):
        """RRF: only RANKS matter, so incomparable scores are never an issue."""
        dense_ids = self.dense(query, fetch)
        lex_ids = self.lexical(query, fetch)

        scores = {}
        for w, ranking in zip(weights, (dense_ids, lex_ids)):
            for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
                scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + w / (rrf_k + rank)

        ranked = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:k]
        return [(doc_id, score) for doc_id, score in ranked]
```

### 2.4 Reranking with a cross-encoder

```python
# pip install sentence-transformers
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

# A cross-encoder scores (query, document) JOINTLY — far more accurate than
# comparing two independently-computed embeddings, and far too slow to run
# over the whole corpus. Hence: retrieve broadly, rerank narrowly.
reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")

def retrieve_and_rerank(retriever, query, fetch=30, top_k=5, min_score=0.0):
    candidates = retriever.search(query, k=fetch)          # (id, score)
    texts = [retriever_text_lookup[cid] for cid, _ in candidates]
    pairs = [(query, t) for t in texts]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs)

    ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates, texts), key=lambda x: -x[0])
    return [{"id": c[0], "text": t, "rerank_score": float(s)}
            for s, c, t in ranked[:top_k] if s >= min_score]
```

The cost: ~30 cross-encoder forward passes per query, roughly 50–150 ms on CPU. Budget it, and measure the recall gain — it is usually worth it.

### 2.5 Contextual retrieval

```python
"""Prepend an LLM-generated context blurb to each chunk before embedding.
   Anthropic reported large retrieval-failure reductions from this."""
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

context_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "<document>\n{document}\n</document>\n\n"
    "Here is a chunk from that document:\n<chunk>\n{chunk}\n</chunk>\n\n"
    "Write 1-2 short sentences situating this chunk within the overall document, "
    "so it can be understood and retrieved on its own. Answer with only that context."
)
contextualiser = context_prompt | model | StrOutputParser()

def contextualise_chunks(document: str, chunks: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for c in chunks:
        blurb = contextualiser.invoke({"document": document[:8000], "chunk": c})
        out.append(f"{blurb}\n\n{c}")       # embed THIS
    return out
```

Cost note: one LLM call per chunk at ingest time. With prompt caching on the document this is cheap, and it is a one-off cost amortised over every future query.

### 2.6 Corrective RAG — grade retrieval, fall back if poor

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class Grade(BaseModel):
    relevant: bool = Field(description="Does this document help answer the question?")
    reason: str

grader = (ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Question: {question}\n\nDocument:\n{document}\n\n"
    "Does this document contain information that helps answer the question?")
    | model.with_structured_output(Grade))

def corrective_retrieve(retriever, question, k=5, web_search_fn=None):
    docs = retriever.search(question, k=k)
    graded = [(d, grader.invoke({"question": question, "document": d["text"]}))
              for d in docs]
    kept = [d for d, g in graded if g.relevant]

    if len(kept) < 2 and web_search_fn:
        print("[CRAG] local retrieval insufficient — falling back to web search")
        kept.extend(web_search_fn(question))
    return kept
```

### 2.7 Permission-filtered retrieval

```python
def retrieve_for_user(collection, query: str, user, k=5):
    """Filter at the DATABASE, never in the prompt.

    The model must never see a document the user cannot access — a prompt
    instruction to 'not reveal' it is not a security control.
    """
    where = {"$or": [
        {"visibility": "public"},
        {"team": {"$in": user.teams}},
        {"owner": user.id},
    ]}
    res = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=k, where=where,
                           include=["documents", "metadatas", "distances"])
    return list(zip(res["documents"][0], res["metadatas"][0], res["distances"][0]))
```

---

## 3. Use Case — an internal knowledge assistant, and the four things that fixed it

A 900-person company built a RAG assistant over their wiki, Google Docs, Slack archive and Jira. First version: naive chunking, dense-only retrieval, top-5, no reranking. Users called it "confidently useless."

**Diagnosis, using §1.3's taxonomy.** They labelled 80 real queries with the chunks that actually contained the answer, then ran §2.1:

```
recall@5  = 0.41      ← failure point 2 dominates
recall@20 = 0.78
faithfulness (of answered queries) = 0.88
refusal accuracy = 0.15               ← almost never admitted ignorance
```

The generation was fine. **Retrieval was the bottleneck, and the refusal behaviour was the safety problem.**

**Four changes, in the order they applied them and what each bought:**

1. **Hybrid retrieval** (dense + BM25, RRF). Recall@5 → 0.58. Biggest single win. Jira ticket IDs and service names are lexical, and dense embeddings simply do not preserve them.
2. **Reranking** — fetch 30, cross-encode, keep 5. Recall@5 → 0.74. Note this works *because* recall@20 was already 0.78 — the reranker can only promote documents retrieval already found.
3. **Similarity floor + explicit refusal path.** Refusal accuracy → 0.89. This changed user trust more than any accuracy gain, because people could finally tell when to believe it.
4. **Permission filtering.** Not a quality change — a compliance requirement they had initially missed. HR documents were retrievable by everyone.

**What did *not* help:** a bigger generation model (they tested it; +0.01 on faithfulness, 4× the cost), and a larger context window stuffed with top-20 (worse, due to "lost in the middle" — see §4).

**The transferable lesson:** measure retrieval and generation separately, fix retrieval first, and treat refusal as a first-class metric.

---

## 4. Worked Example — diagnosing a RAG failure properly

A user reports: *"It said our deploy window is Thursday. It's Tuesday."*

### Step 1 — reproduce and inspect the retrieval, before anything else

```python
question = "when is our deploy window?"
hits = retriever.search(question, k=5)
for i, h in enumerate(hits, 1):
    print(f"{i}. [{h['id']}] score={h['score']:.3f}")
    print(f"   {h['text'][:150]}\n")
```

Output:
```
1. [legacy-runbook-0003] score=0.612
   Deployments are scheduled for Thursday evenings during the maintenance window...
2. [runbook-0001] score=0.589
   Production deployments run every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC...
3. [onboarding-0012] score=0.501
   New engineers should shadow a deploy in their first week...
```

**Immediately this is not failure point 4 (extraction) — it is a retrieval ranking problem plus a data problem.** The correct chunk *was* retrieved, at rank 2. The model quite reasonably used rank 1.

### Step 2 — identify the root cause

The corpus contains a **stale document**. `legacy-runbook.md` describes a process abandoned 18 months ago. Nobody deleted it.

This is the most common real-world RAG failure and it is not a model problem at all. It is a **corpus hygiene** problem.

### Step 3 — the fix hierarchy, cheapest first

**(a) Fix the data.** Delete or archive the stale document. Always the first move.
```python
collection.delete(where={"source": "legacy-runbook.md"})
```

**(b) Add temporal metadata and filter or boost on it.**
```python
metadata = {"source": ..., "last_updated": "2024-03-01", "status": "archived"}

res = collection.query(query_texts=[q], n_results=5,
                       where={"status": {"$ne": "archived"}})
```

**(c) Add a reranker.** A cross-encoder scoring `(query, document)` jointly would likely rank the Tuesday chunk above the Thursday one, because "deploy window" matches "Production deployments run every Tuesday" more specifically than "scheduled for Thursday evenings during the maintenance window."

**(d) Surface conflicts to the user.** When top results disagree, say so rather than silently picking one:
```python
CONFLICT_PROMPT = """If the retrieved documents contain conflicting information,
do not pick one. State the conflict, cite both sources with their dates, and
recommend the user verify."""
```

**(e) Include dates in the context block**, so the model can reason about recency:
```python
context = "\n\n".join(
    f"[{m['source']}, updated {m.get('last_updated','unknown')}]\n{d}"
    for d, m in zip(docs, metas))
```

### Step 4 — the second bug hiding in this example

Look again at the scores: **0.612 vs 0.589**. A 0.023 margin. Even with the stale document removed, that margin tells you the retrieval is fragile — add 10,000 documents and rankings at this margin are effectively random.

Log the top-1/top-2 score gap in production. A consistently small gap means your embeddings are not discriminating well on your corpus, which points at chunk size (Lesson 2 §4) or the embedding model.

### Step 5 — the anti-fix, and why it fails

The instinct is to raise `k` from 5 to 20 so "more context can't hurt." It can.

**Lost in the middle** (Liu et al., 2023): models attend most reliably to the *beginning* and *end* of their context, and reliably worse to the middle. Stuffing 20 chunks pushes the answer into the dead zone, dilutes attention, and costs 4× the tokens.

**Retrieve broadly, rerank hard, pass few.** Fetch 30, rerank, pass 3–5, and put the highest-scoring chunk **last** in the context (closest to the question) or first — both positions beat the middle.

---

## 5. Practice

1. **Build the eval set first.** Take 40 real questions about your corpus. Label the chunk IDs that contain each answer. Include 10 unanswerable questions. This is 2 hours of tedious work and it is the highest-value thing in this module.
2. Run §2.1 on your Lesson 2 collection. Report recall@1/3/5/10, MRR and nDCG. **This is your baseline** — every improvement from here is measured against it.
3. Implement hybrid retrieval (§2.3). Re-run the eval. Report the recall@5 delta. Then find one query where dense wins and one where BM25 wins, and explain each.
4. Add reranking (§2.4). Re-run. Report the delta and the added latency. Compute the recall@5 as a fraction of recall@30 — that ratio tells you how much headroom the reranker has.
5. **Query transformation comparison.** For the same eval set, compare: baseline, multi-query, HyDE, and decomposition. Report recall@5 and cost per query for each. Which is worth its cost?
6. Implement contextual retrieval (§2.5) on 200 chunks. Measure the recall change and the one-off ingestion cost.
7. **Reproduce "lost in the middle."** Put the correct chunk at position 1, 5, and 10 of a 10-chunk context. Measure answer accuracy at each position over 20 questions. Plot it.
8. Implement corrective RAG (§2.6) with a web-search fallback. Test on 10 questions your corpus cannot answer. Does it correctly fall back?
9. **Permission filtering.** Build a collection with three visibility levels and three users. Write a test asserting user A can never retrieve user B's private documents — including via a prompt-injection attempt.
10. **Write the decision doc.** For a RAG system you'd actually build: state the corpus, the update frequency, the permission model, the chunking strategy, the retrieval architecture, the eval metrics and their targets, and the refusal policy. Two pages. This is the deliverable that matters professionally.

---

## 6. Resources

**Papers**
- Lewis et al., *Retrieval-Augmented Generation* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
- Gao et al., *RAG for LLMs: A Survey* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997
- Barnett et al., *Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856
- Liu et al., *Lost in the Middle* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172
- Gao et al., *HyDE: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496
- Asai et al., *Self-RAG* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511
- Yan et al., *Corrective RAG* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884
- Edge et al., *GraphRAG* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130
- Es et al., *RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of RAG* — https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217

**Engineering**
- Anthropic, *Introducing Contextual Retrieval* — https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval
- LangChain RAG from scratch — https://github.com/langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch
- RAGAS — https://docs.ragas.io/

**Tools**
- Cross-encoder rerankers — https://sbert.net/docs/pretrained_cross-encoders.html
- BEIR retrieval benchmark — https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir
